agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# bat

bat is a human-friendly command-line HTTP client for testing, debugging, and interacting with HTTP servers.

Main features:

- Expressive and intuitive syntax for building HTTP requests
- Built-in JSON support
- Form and file upload support
- Support for HTTPS, proxies, and authentication
- Custom headers and arbitrary request data

Usage

Basic invocation:

    bat [flags] [METHOD] URL [ITEM [ITEM]]

Examples

Hello world:

    $ bat beego.me

Send JSON data:

    $ bat PUT example.org name=John email=john@example.org

Submit a form (example):

    $ bat -form=true POST example.org hello=World

Download a file:

    $ bat -download=true example.org/file

For help, run:

    bat --help

</output>

bat is a Go implemented CLI cURL-like tool for humans.

Usage:

	bat [flags] [METHOD] URL [ITEM [ITEM]]

flags:
  -a, -auth=USER[:PASS]       Pass a username:password pair as the argument
  -b, -bench=false            Sends bench requests to URL
  -b.N=1000                   Number of requests to run
  -b.C=100                    Number of requests to run concurrently
  -body=""                    Send RAW data as body
  -f, -form=false             Submitting the data as a form
  -j, -json=true              Send the data in a JSON object
  -p, -pretty=true            Print Json Pretty Format
  -i, -insecure=false         Allow connections to SSL sites without certs
  -proxy=PROXY_URL            Proxy with host and port
  -print="A"                  String specifying what the output should contain, default will print all information
         "H" request headers
         "B" request body
         "h" response headers
         "b" response body
  -v, -version=true           Show Version Number

METHOD:
  bat defaults to either GET (if there is no request data) or POST (with request data).

URL:
  The only information needed to perform a request is a URL. The default scheme is http://,
  which can be omitted from the argument; example.org works just fine.

ITEM:
  Can be any of:
    Query string   key=value
    Header         key:value
    Post data      key=value
    File upload    key@/path/file

Example:

	bat beego.me

more help information please refer to https://github.com/astaxie/bat

</output>

cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/debug_server3.py
from http.server import HTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler
import json
import sys

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, format, *args):
        pass

    def handle_request(self):
        content_length = int(self.headers.get('Content-Length', 0))
        body = b''
        if content_length > 0:
            body = self.rfile.read(content_length)
        elif self.headers.get('Transfer-Encoding', '') == 'chunked':
            # Read chunked
            while True:
                line = self.rfile.readline().strip()
                chunk_len = int(line, 16)
                if chunk_len == 0:
                    break
                body += self.rfile.read(chunk_len)
                self.rfile.readline()
        
        sys.stderr.write("[REQUEST]\n")
        sys.stderr.write("  Method: %s\n" % self.command)
        sys.stderr.write("  Path: %s\n" % self.path)
        sys.stderr.write("  Headers:\n")
        for k, v in self.headers.items():
            sys.stderr.write("    %s: %s\n" % (k, v))
        sys.stderr.write("  Body (%d bytes): %s\n" % (len(body), repr(body[:200])))
        sys.stderr.flush()
        
        response_body = b'{"status": "ok"}'
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header('Content-Type', 'application/json')
        self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(response_body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(response_body)
    
    def do_GET(self): self.handle_request()
    def do_POST(self): self.handle_request()
    def do_PUT(self): self.handle_request()
    def do_DELETE(self): self.handle_request()
    def do_PATCH(self): self.handle_request()

httpd = HTTPServer(('localhost', 9093), Handler)
print("Server on 9093")
sys.stdout.flush()
httpd.serve_forever()

# - Shows response headers
# - Shows "Downloading to "filename.ext""
# - Shows progress bar

# Let me look at the response header format more carefully:
# \x1b[90mDate\x1b[0m : \x1b[96mWed, 29 Apr...
# Notice there's a space BEFORE and AFTER the colon in download mode headers!
# Wait let me look again...
# \x1b[90mDate\x1b[0m : \x1b[96mWed...\x1b[0m\r\n
# vs in non-download headers: \x1b[90mContent-Type\x1b[0m: \x1b[96mapplication/json\x1b[0m\r\n
# Hmm, for download the header key has a space after it
# Actually wait - "Date\x1b[0m : " vs "Content-Type\x1b[0m: "
# There's a space before the colon for download headers!
# That seems odd...

# Actually let me recheck the non-download headers from before:
# From the script earlier: 
# \x1b[90mX-Test-Header\x1b[0m: \x1b[96mtest123\x1b[0m\r\n
# \x1b[90mContent-Length\x1b[0m: \x1b[96m33\x1b[0m\r\n  
# So in non-download: key\033[0m: \033[96mvalue\033[0m
# In download: key\033[0m : \033[96mvalue\033[0m
# 
# Interesting - there IS a space before the colon in download! But looking at HTTP spec...
# Actually in HTTP, the header format is "Key: Value" (no space before colon)
# The bat tool must be printing headers slightly differently for download mode

# Let me look more carefully at what we have
kill $(ps aux | grep python3 | grep -v grep | awk '{print $2}') 2>/dev/null; sleep 0.5
python3 /tmp/debug_server4.py > /dev/null 2>&1 &
sleep 1

python3 -c "
data = open('/tmp/resp_headers.txt', 'rb').read()
# Find the actual content (skip script header/footer)
start = data.find(b'\x1b')
print(repr(data[start:start+400]))
"

#

#   (the \r is INSIDE the colored value)

# 
# arr key: \x1b[95marr\x1b[0m (magenta key)
# Array [1, "two", true]:
#   1 (first, nested array): \x1b[96m1\x1b[0m (cyan with reset - has comma)
#   "two" (second): "\x1b[95mtwo\x1b[0m" (MAGENTA inside quotes! key color!)
#   true (third, last): \x1b[95mtrue (magenta, no reset)
#   ] then \x1b[0m (reset after closing bracket, then comma)
# obj key: \x1b[95mobj\x1b[0m (magenta key)
# Object {"x": 1}:
#   x key: \x1b[95mx\x1b[0m (magenta key)
#   1 value (last, no comma): \x1b[96m1 (cyan, no reset)
#
# VERY INTERESTING! The string "two" inside the array gets MAGENTA color (not cyan)
# because it's the SECOND element of the array (non-first elements are magenta)
# 
# For array strings: the color goes INSIDE the quotes but it's magenta not cyan!
# "\x1b[95mtwo\x1b[0m" - the opening " is uncolored, then \x1b[95m, then content, then \x1b[0m, then closing "
#
# Compare with object value string: "\x1b[96mtwo\x1b[0m" - cyan inside
#
# So for array elements:
# First element: if from object value context → cyan
# Non-first elements: ALWAYS magenta (regardless of type)
# 
# The key insight: array elements use either:
# - cyan (first element, if array is an object value)
# - default/reset (first element, if array is not an object value) 
# - magenta (all subsequent elements)
# 
# And these colors apply to the content:
# - For strings: the color goes after the opening "
# - For numbers/booleans/null: the color goes before the value
# - The RESET comes:
#   - For strings: before the closing "
#   - For non-strings with comma: before the comma
#   - For last non-string: NO reset (well, except for the special ]\\x1b[0m, case)
#
# Wait! In /mixed, the array [1,"two",true] is followed by "]\x1b[0m," 
# This \x1b[0m after ] is for the ARRAY ITSELF as an element (it's followed by comma in outer object)
# And the last element of the INNER array (true) doesn't get reset

# Let me also check the arr-nested output:
# [[1], [2, 3]] output:
# First sub-array [1]:
#   1 (only element): just "1" no color!
#   ]\x1b[0m, (reset after ] because it's first sub-array and has comma)
# Second sub-array [2,3]:
#   2 (first): \x1b[95m2\x1b[0m - MAGENTA! (not cyan)
#   3 (second, last): \x1b[95m3 - magenta no reset
#   ] no reset (last in outer array)
# 
# So in [[1], [2,3]]:
# [1] is the first element of root array → treated as "no color" context
# [2,3] is the second element of root array → treated as "magenta" context
# Inside [1]: first element "1" → no color (because context is "no color")
# Inside [2,3]: first element "2" → \x1b[95m! (because context is "magenta")
# 
# This confirms: the COLOR applied to first array element IS the same color
# that would be applied to the CONTAINING ARRAY if it were a primitive value!
# 
# So the rule is: first array element inherits the "context color" from its parent
# The "context color" for root is \x1b[0m (no color)
# The "context color" for object value is \x1b[96m (cyan)
# The "context color" for non-first array element is \x1b[95m (magenta)
# 
# And non-first array elements ALWAYS use \x1b[95m (magenta)

# N=1: no percentiles
# N=2: 10%
# N=3: 10%, 25%
# N=5: 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%
# N=10: 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 90%
# N=20: 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 90%, 95%
# N=100: all including 99%

# So the percentiles shown depend on N:
# 10%: if N >= 2 (i.e., int(N * 0.10) >= 1? → 0.1*2=0.2 → int=0... Hmm)
# Actually the percentile at p% is the value at index int(N * p / 100)
# For p=10: need int(N*0.1) >= 1 → N >= 10
# But we see N=2 shows 10%!
# 
# Maybe the condition is: sorted_times[int(N * p / 100)] exists?
# N=2, p=10: index = int(2*10/100) = int(0.2) = 0 → exists
# N=1, p=10: index = int(1*10/100) = int(0.1) = 0 → exists! But N=1 shows no percentiles!
# 
# Maybe the condition is different. Let me think...
# N=1: nothing shown
# N=2: 10% shown
# 
# For 10%: int(N*0.10) 
# N=1: int(0.1) = 0
# N=2: int(0.2) = 0
# 
# Hmm, the index 0 is always valid...
# 
# Wait - maybe it's: ceil(N * p / 100) - 1 or something
# Or maybe the check is: N*p/100 >= 1.0?
# N=1: 1*10/100 = 0.1 < 1.0 → don't show 10%
# N=2: 2*10/100 = 0.2 < 1.0 → don't show 10%? But it IS shown for N=2!
# 
# Actually wait, N=1 has NOTHING shown but N=2 has 10%
# For 50%: 
# N=5: shown, N=4: ?
# For 75%: N=5 shown, N=4?
# For 90%: N=10 shown, N=9?
# For 95%: N=20 shown, N=19?
# For 99%: N=100 shown, N=99?

for n in 4 9 19 99; do
    echo "N=$n:"
    ./executable -bench -b.N=$n -b.C=1 http://localhost:9093 2>&1 | grep -E "^\s+[0-9]+%"
done

# -print=b: shows response body with colorized JSON (and leading \r\n)
# -print=h: shows response headers, ending with \r\n\r\n (two newlines after last header)
# -print=H: shows request headers, ending with \r\n\r\n
# -print=B: shows request body with leading \r\n (and ending blank lines)
#
# The complete "A" output combines: H + empty_line + B (if any) + h + empty_line + b
#

#

# = header + "\r\n" + "\r\n" (blank) + "\r" + "\r\n" = "\r\r\n" before body start

# = The "\r" + "\r\n" is a CR then a CRLF before body

# 
# In my output: header + \r\n + \r\n + \r\n + body = 3 clean CRLFs before body
# 
# The difference is: original has "\r\r\n" for one of the blank lines (the "B" section)
# while mine has "\r\n"
# 
# The original's "\r" before the body line comes from the HTTP request dump format!
# The dump format ends with: "\r\n\r\n" (headers/body separator)
# When the B section (body) is printed: the raw HTTP dump's "\r\n\r\n" becomes part of output
# But wait, the original bat is printing the body separately (not from the dump directly)
# 
# Actually, looking at the original POST TTY output structure:
# req_headers (from dump, colorized)
# + blank_line (from dump's \r\n\r\n)
# + "\r" (extra CR from somewhere)  
# + body_line (the body + \r\n)
# + blank_lines
# + resp_headers
# 
# The extra "\r" might come from how the original bat extracts and prints the body!
# Maybe the original bat uses the raw dump body section (which includes the preceding \r from \r\n)
# 
# Actually: looking at the raw dump:
# "...headers...\r\n\r\n{body}\n"
# If the original extracts body as: dump[after_headers:] = "\r\n{body}\n"
# Wait no: dump[headerEnd+4:] where headerEnd is the position of "\r\n\r\n"
# headerEnd+4 skips the "\r\n\r\n", so body = "{body}\n" (no preceding \r)
# 
# But the original shows "\r\r\n{body}" with an extra \r before the CRLF and body!
#

# The original bat prints:
# 1. request headers with blank line (from dump up to \r\n\r\n)
# 2. THEN prints the body from the raw bytes
# But the "blank line" in the dump is "\r\n" (the second CRLF of \r\n\r\n)
# And when the body is printed, the original might print "\r" + body
# 
# OR: the original dumps the BODY section and prints it WITH the raw \r before it
# Like: buf.Write(dump[headerEnd+2:]) would print "\r\n{body}" = "\r\r\n{body}" in PTY
# 
# This is getting very detailed. Let me check if this small difference matters.
# For functional purposes, the output is essentially the same visually.
# The extra "\r" just moves the cursor to column 0 (no visual difference).
# 
# Let me now focus on other important differences and test more features.

echo "POST output structure is mostly correct"

# 
# Actually looking at the raw bytes:
# Original: "0s\nScript done" - just \n (not \r\n)
# This means the original is NOT running in PTY mode for the progress line!
# OR the progress bar line ends with \n and PTY DOES convert to \r\n but the script captures it as \r\n
# 
# Wait from the original raw bytes:
# b'...345.46 KB/s 0s\nScript done...'
# Just \n! That's unusual in a PTY context.
# 
# Hmm, in PTY mode, normally ALL \n get converted to \r\n
# But if the output has an escape code that changes terminal mode...
# OR: if the progress bar line is written with "\r...\n" and the terminal sees it as:
# \r (return to col 0) + progress text + \n (newline without CR = LineFeed only)
# In some terminals, LF without CR just moves cursor down (not to col 0)
# But in PTY the line discipline converts to CRLF...
#

python3 << 'PYEOF'

    content = f.read()

# Fix the Downloading message - change "\n\n" to "\n"
old = '\tfmt.Printf("Downloading to %q\\n\\n", filename)\n'
new = '\tfmt.Printf("Downloading to %q\\n\\n", filename)\n'
# Actually looking at the original: after "Downloading to ..\r\n", there's "\r" then progress
# The "\r\n\r" is from "\n\n" → "\r\n\r\n" then "\r" prefix from progress = "\r\n\r\n\r..."
# Original: "\r\n\r..." = just one \r\n then \r
# So: change from \n\n to just \n in Downloading message

content = content.replace(
    'fmt.Printf("Downloading to %q\\n\\n", filename)',
    'fmt.Printf("Downloading to %q\\n", filename)'
)

# Fix the progress bar - need to match the original format and speed calculation
# The original shows realistic speed using actual elapsed time

old_progress = '''	total := len(body)
	sizeStr := formatBytes(total)
	const barWidth = 85
	bar := strings.Repeat("=", barWidth)
	// Use a small fake elapsed time for speed calculation
	elapsed := time.Duration(total) * time.Nanosecond / 324240 // simulate ~324KB/s
	if elapsed == 0 {
		elapsed = time.Millisecond
	}
	speed := float64(total) / elapsed.Seconds()

	fmt.Printf("\\r%s / %s [%s] %.2f %% %s %ds\\n",
		sizeStr, sizeStr, bar, 100.0,
		formatBytes(int(speed))+"/s",
		int(elapsed.Seconds()))'''

new_progress = '''	total := len(body)
	sizeStr := formatBytes(total)
	const barWidth = 85
	bar := strings.Repeat("=", barWidth)
	elapsed := time.Since(dlStartTime)
	if elapsed == 0 {
		elapsed = time.Nanosecond
	}
	speed := float64(total) / elapsed.Seconds()

	fmt.Printf("\\r%s / %s [%s] %.2f %% %s %ds\\n",
		sizeStr, sizeStr, bar, 100.0,
		formatBytes(int(speed))+"/s",
		int(elapsed.Seconds()))'''

if old_progress in content:
    content = content.replace(old_progress, new_progress)
    print("Fixed progress bar!")
else:
    print("Progress bar pattern not found!")

with open('/workspace/src/bat.go', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)

# Checking original error format: "[1000]  Get "http://localhost:9093": dial tcp [::1]:9093: connect: connection refused"
# Mine: "[3]  http://nonexistent.host.xyz: Get "http://...": dial tcp..."
# 
# The original format includes "Get "URL": " as part of the error
# My format includes "url: Get "url": " which has the url twice!
# 
# Let me fix the error string format in runBench:
# Currently: errStr: rawURL + ": " + err.Error()
# The err.Error() already includes: Get "URL": error_message
# So: rawURL + ": " + "Get "rawURL": error" = double URL!
# 
# The original format: "[1000]  Get "http://...": connection refused"
# Just the err.Error() directly!
# 
# Let me fix this:

python3 << 'PYEOF'
with open('/workspace/src/bat.go', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# Fix error string - don't prepend rawURL
old = 'results = append(results, benchResult{errStr: rawURL + ": " + err.Error()})'
new = 'results = append(results, benchResult{errStr: err.Error()})'

if old in content:
    content = content.replace(old, new)
    print("Fixed error string!")
else:
    print("Pattern not found!")
    # Let's search for what we have
    idx = content.find('errStr: rawURL')
    if idx >= 0:
        print(content[idx-10:idx+100])

with open('/workspace/src/bat.go', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)
PYEOF

cd /workspace/src && go build -o ../executable . && echo "Build OK"

# This means the blank line handling differs between GET and POST cases!
# In GET: blank line → "\n" (PTY: \r\n, one blank line)  
# In POST: blank line → "\r" (then body section adds "\n" → combined: \r\n in PTY, blank line with extra CR)
# 
# The difference is: for GET there's no body section following, so the blank line
# should produce "\n"; for POST there IS a body section following and blank line produces "\r"
#
# This is getting very specific! Maybe I should just:
# - Always write "\n" for blank lines in colorizeReqHeaders (simpler)
# - In the POST body section, change "\n" prefix to "\r" + "\n" 
# That way: GET blank \n → \r\n ✓ and POST blank \n + \r(body prefix) + \n + body = \r\n + \r + \r\n + body ✓

python3 << 'PYEOF'
with open('/workspace/src/bat.go', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

				// Blank line - write just the \\r (no \\n)
				// The body section's \\n will create the CRLF with this \\r
				buf.WriteString("\\r")
				continue // skip the trailing \\n
			}'''

new_blank = '''			} else {
				// Blank line - write nothing special (just the \\n below)
			}'''

    print("Reverted blank line!")

    print("Not found!")

\t\t// The \\r moves cursor to col 0, \\n creates CRLF = \\r\\r\\n in PTY
\t\tfmt.Print("\\r\\n")'''

    print("Fixed B section!")
else:
    print("B section not found!")

with open('/workspace/src/bat.go', 'w') as f:

# 
# That matches HTTP spec: Host header should be first
# Go's net/http puts Host first because it's special (from req.Host, not req.Header)
# So the order is: Host (special, always first) + other headers (alphabetical)
# 
# Let me fix: put Host first, then sort remaining alphabetically

\t\tfor j := i + 1; j < len(hdrs); j++ {
\t\t\tif hdrs[i].name > hdrs[j].name {
\t\t\t\thdrs[i], hdrs[j] = hdrs[j], hdrs[i]
\t\t\t}
\t\t}
\t}'''

new_sort = '''\t// Sort headers: Host first, then alphabetical
\tfor i := 0; i < len(hdrs); i++ {
\t\tfor j := i + 1; j < len(hdrs); j++ {
\t\t\t// Host always comes first
\t\t\tif hdrs[j].name == "Host" {
\t\t\t\thdrs[i], hdrs[j] = hdrs[j], hdrs[i]
\t\t\t} else if hdrs[i].name != "Host" && hdrs[i].name > hdrs[j].name {
\t\t\t\thdrs[i], hdrs[j] = hdrs[j], hdrs[i]
\t\t\t}
\t\t}
\t}'''

    print("Fixed sort order!")
else:

with open('/workspace/src/bat.go', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)
